evidence: TaskManagementService.addTask: checks the project exists, calls domain createTask/assignTask, then this.tasks.save(task). This is orchestration through a repository port.
TaskManagementService.listTasks: uses domain isTaskStatus to check the filter, then calls this.tasks.findByProject. The status rule itself stays in the domain.
TaskManagementService.markDone: hands the state change to domain markTaskDone and only saves the result.
requireProject/requireTask/requireUser: look up the entity through a repository port and throw domain NotFoundError if it is missing. No storage details appear.
IdGenerator interface: a port owned by the application layer, implemented by infrastructure UuidGenerator.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: The file holds only use-case coordination, which is the job of the application layer. UserService and TaskManagementService fetch aggregates through repository ports that are injected into them. They call domain factories and functions (createUser, createProject, createTask, assignTask, markTaskDone, isTaskStatus) and save the results. Existence checks (requireProject, requireTask, requireUser) throw domain NotFoundError. The input DTOs CreateTaskInput and ListTasksInput are converted into domain types at the use-case boundary: the dueDate string becomes a Date, and the status filter is checked with the domain predicate isTaskStatus. This is normal application-layer input handling, not business rules. IdGenerator is an application-owned port, and infrastructure implements it. The file has no persistence code, no HTTP or other transport handling, and no framework code. Business rules such as the valid task statuses, the state change to done and assignment live in the domain functions this file calls.
